title: TPG-backed NewQuest offloads Rs 200 Cr Shadowfax stake in a bulk deal
summary:
TPG-backed NewQuest Asia Fund IV has offloaded another 1.36% stake in logistics startup Shadowfax for around Rs 200 crore through a bulk deal on the BSE.
According to exchange data, NewQuest sold 80 lakh shares at Rs 250.03 apiece, while OxBow Master Fund bought 47.85 lakh shares at Rs 250 each, worth around Rs 119.6 crore.
The transaction follows a similar deal in August, when NewQuest sold 1.25 crore Shadowfax shares at Rs 240.46 apiece for around Rs 300.6 crore. OxBow Master Fund had bought 69.32 lakh shares at Rs 240.25 apiece in that transaction worth Rs 166.5 crore.
As of June 2026, NewQuest held an 11.53% stake in Shadowfax. Across the two transactions, it has sold around 2.05 crore shares worth over Rs 500 crore, while Oxbow acquired a 2% stake in the company.
The latest deal comes as Shadowfax continues to see secondary-market activity following its public listing.
In Q1 FY27, Shadowfax recorded a 65% year-on-year growth in operating revenue to Rs 1,358 crore. Its profit also surged more than eightfold to Rs 65 crore during the quarter.
At the end of Tuesday’s trading session, Shadowfax's share price closed at around Rs 249.8 on BSE, valuing the company at Rs 14,656 crore (approximately $1.54 billion).

title: Bajaj Finance acquires 5% stake in TrueFan AI
summary:
Bajaj Finance, part of Bajaj Finserv, has acquired a 5% stake in TrueFan AI, an AI-powered video generation platform.
The Gurugram-based startup had previously secured $10 million in a Series A funding round led by Baring Private Equity Partners India and Z3 Partners in June this year.
Founded in 2020 by Devender Bindal, Nimish Goel, and Nevaid Aggarwal, TrueFan AI offers an enterprise AI video platform that uses generative AI to create hyper-personalized, studio-quality videos and avatars from a single recording. The platform helps more than 100 enterprise clients scale video marketing across global markets.
TrueFan AI plans to expand beyond India into Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and the US. The company says it has already witnessed demand from these markets. Its deep-learning models synthesize facial dynamics, gestures, and voice to generate up to 500,000 localized videos per minute across more than 175 languages.
The startup serves over 100 enterprise customers, including HDFC Bank, Bajaj Finance, Zomato, Cipla, and BharatPe. The platform enables companies to create AI-powered personalized videos at scale through celebrity avatars, business leaders, and enterprise spokespersons.
The company’s flagship product, TF Studio, enables brands to create personalized messages in bulk, localize content for different markets, and deploy lifelike brand ambassador avatars.
TrueFan AI reported revenue of Rs 17.1 crore (approximately $2 million) in FY25. Revenue grew 131% year-on-year.
Bajaj Finance has deployed TrueFan’s platform at scale, generating millions of personalized videos for customer engagement and dealer enablement initiatives. It also supports Bajaj Finance’s broader strategy of deploying AI-led automation and personalization across its digital ecosystem.

title: Kuku to build 1,000-member AI team ahead of Rs 3,500 Cr IPO
summary:
Kuku Technologies, the parent company of Kuku FM and Kuku TV, is building a 1,000-member AI-led content production unit as it looks to scale its microdrama business globally, according to people familiar with the matter. 
The company has already hired nearly 200 people for the Mumbai-based unit and plans to expand the team to around 1,000 by the end of the current financial year, the sources said. 
The hiring comes as Kuku has confidentially filed draft IPO papers with market regulator SEBI for a public issue of up to Rs 3,500 crore. The company is targeting a valuation of around $1.8 billion through the IPO.
Kuku is bringing writers, filmmakers and engineers into the new AI-native unit. Writers will develop stories and dialogues, filmmakers will focus on visual direction, while engineers will build AI systems for areas such as narrative continuity across long-running series.
Kuku expects AI to cut microdrama production costs to 30-50% of China’s, with production costing under $100 per minute versus over $150 in China, sources said. AI-led production can also help one person produce around 20 minutes of usable video a day, compared with about a minute through traditional shoots. 
Kuku declined to comment when contacted.
Founded in 2018 by IIT alumni Lal Chand Bisu, Vinod Kumar, and Vikas Goyal, Kuku operates vernacular audio platform Kuku FM, short-video app Kuku TV, and edutainment platform Guru. Across its platforms, Kuku claims to have over 10 million active paying subscribers, 400 million app downloads, and a content library of more than 60,000 hours spanning several Indian languages. 
The company has raised over $150 million from investors including Fundamentum Partnership, Krafton, Vertex Ventures, Granite Asia, IFC, Paramark Ventures, India Quotient, and 3one4 Capital. Former Indian cricket captain MS Dhoni is also among its backers.
According to sources, Kuku's revenue grew nearly sevenfold to more than Rs 1,400 crore in FY26 from Rs 240 crore in the fiscal year ending March 2025.

title: Navam Capital leads Rs 22 Cr round in DigitalPaani
summary:
AI-powered water infrastructure platform DigitalPaani has raised Rs 22 crore in a funding round led by Navam Capital, with participation from Enzia Ventures, Chakra Growth Capital, 3one4 Capital, Momentum Capital, Achieving Women Entrepreneurs Early Growth Fund, and Echo River Capital.
The fresh funds will be used to expand market penetration across the industrial and municipal sectors, scale operations to serve its growing institutional customer base, and begin international expansion, DigitalPaani said in a press release.
Co-founded in 2020 by Mansi Jain and Rajesh Jain, DigitalPaani provides an operating system for water and wastewater infrastructure. Its platform combines AI-driven insights with real-time asset monitoring to help utilities, municipalities, and enterprises improve water recycling, reduce operational losses, and prevent equipment failures.
According to the Gurugram-based company, its platform analyses real-time operational data against how each asset is designed to operate, identifies inefficiencies and automates actions related to equipment, maintenance, teams, and inventory.
DigitalPaani said it serves more than 95 facilities, treating over 150 million litres of water daily. Its clients include Britannia, Leela Hotels, Tata Group, and Delhi Jal Board. The company said its deployments have helped transform non-compliant plants into fully operational assets while delivering cost savings of up to 25%. Its revenue has grown nearly sixfold over the past two years.
Ubiqedge is another startup operating in the infrastructure digitisation space. It raised Rs 10 crore in a seed round led by Piper Serica in April this year to scale its AIoT platform for infrastructure, including water systems. The company said its technology has digitised more than 23,000 borewells.
Meanwhile, IIT Madras-incubated Solinas Integrity raised $5.5 million in a Series A1 round in August, led by Mela Ventures and Hero Enterprise Family Office. The startup uses robotics and AI to inspect, clean, and digitise underground water, wastewater, and sanitation infrastructure.

Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS) platform Circolife has raised $4.5 million (around Rs 40.45 crore) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Bharat Jaisinghani, joint managing director of Polycab India. The round also saw participation from a group of individual, fund and family-office investors, including Nitish Mittersain, Intelliquity Ventures, Sumit Jalan, Siddharth Ladsariya, Anand Ladsariya, Anant Goenka, Sky Impact Capital, Rohit Dev, and family offices S N Damani and Vyom Wealth.
The fresh funds will be used to expand its fleet and geographic footprint, scale its in-house installation and service capabilities, and advance its AI-augmented IoT predictive-maintenance and digital twin platform, Circolife said in a press release.
Founded in 2023 by Abhishek Murarka, Tushar Patil and Devanshu Mishra, Circolife owns, installs and services the air-conditioning units it deploys throughout their working life. The startup uses embedded IoT sensors and predictive maintenance to monitor the fleet and refurbishes and redeploys units at the end of their life cycle.
The Thane-based startup said it currently operates across five Indian cities, serving small businesses and enterprise customers across restaurants, hotels, gyms, salons, co-living operators and corporate offices through a subscription-based model for cooling.
Under its subscription model, Circolife installs and maintains the air-conditioning units while customers pay a monthly fee. The company said its units are designed for energy efficiency, while its ownership of the equipment over the contract period allows it to monitor and maintain their performance.
According to Circolife, its units are connected devices equipped with sensors that track temperature, power consumption and gas pressure in real time. This data feeds into a predictive-maintenance system designed to identify potential equipment failures before they result in breakdowns. The startup is also using AI and additional sensors to build digital twins of its deployed devices.
Circolife plans to increase its subscription base fourfold and reach 40,000 units within the next 24 months.
Cooling-as-a-Service is gaining traction within India’s climate-tech and energy-efficiency startup ecosystem, allowing businesses to access air-conditioning and cooling infrastructure without making the upfront capital investment.
Smart Joules, which operates a CaaS model through its JouleCool platform, raised $10 million in Series B funding in December last year from SVL SME Neev II Fund, Waaree Renewable Technologies and Spectrum Impact. The company is using the capital to expand its cooling and energy-efficiency operations across manufacturing, building automation and district cooling.
Other startups exploring the broader cooling-as-a-service and thermal-management space include Tan90, which has raised funding for its thermal-energy-storage solutions and launched a CaaS model for cold-chain businesses.

title: Beverage brand Sorry Sugar raises $1 Mn in seed round
summary:
Gurugram-based beverage brand Sorry Sugar has raised $1 million in a seed funding round led by the Dhanuka family and Amishi London.
The company said the funding will be used to expand its online and offline presence across North India and support new product launches.
Founded this year by Deepak Pathak, Kunal Verma, Shashank Sherawat and Saiyam Malik, Sorry Sugar offers beverages with zero added sugar. Its portfolio includes coffee-based flavours such as Hazel Almond Latte, Silk Chocolate Mocha, Sea Salt Caramel, French Vanilla Cloud and Butter Gooey Toffee.
The company also offers a Rs 399 trial pack containing five flavours, with the amount fully redeemable when upgrading to a larger pack.
Sorry Sugar said its beverages are sweetened with monk fruit and contain fibre. The company is positioning its products as alternatives for consumers looking to reduce their sugar intake.
The brand claims to have generated more than Rs 1 crore in revenue in its first month and currently operates three offline stores across Gurugram and Delhi. It is targeting an ARR of more than Rs 60 crore by the end of the current financial year and plans to expand across D2C, quick commerce and offline retail channels.
The company also plans to launch a range of zero-added-sugar gelatos sweetened with monk fruit.
The funding comes amid growing activity in India’s functional and clean-label beverage segment. Peping, a functional beverage startup offering prebiotic fizzy drinks and probiotic digestive shots, raised Rs 2.5 crore from IAN Angel Fund in March this year. Swizzle, a clean-label beverage startup, raised Rs 2 crore in seed funding in December last year. title: Whatfix appoints co-founder Vara Kumar as CEO following Khadim Batti’s demise
summary:
Enterprise software startup Whatfix has appointed cofounder Vara Kumar as its chief executive officer (CEO), effective immediately. Kumar succeeds cofounder Khadim Batti, following his demise on September 1.
Kumar co-founded Whatfix with Batti in 2014 and has led the company’s product and research strategy. In his new role, he will oversee the company’s operations and growth alongside the existing executive leadership team and board.
Whatfix said its operations across regions will continue under the new leadership.
The Bengaluru and San Jose-based company operates a digital adoption platform that combines AI, analytics, simulation training and intelligent agents to help enterprises use software more effectively.
Whatfix claims to serve more than 600 enterprises globally, including over 80 Fortune 500 companies such as Shell, Schneider Electric, Mercedes-Benz, Heineken and UPS Supply Chain Solutions.
The company is backed by investors including Warburg Pincus, SoftBank Vision Fund 2, Dragoneer, Peak XV Partners, Eight Roads and Cisco Investments.

title: Gaming tech startup ARC raises Rs 10.5 Cr in pre-seed round
summary:
Kerala-based gaming technology company ARC has raised Rs 10.5 crore in a pre-seed funding round led by Chimera VC and MIXI Global Investments, with participation from Dhruv Vohra, Director at Meta APAC, in his personal capacity. 
The fresh capital will be used to accelerate hardware engineering, product validation, manufacturing and supply-chain readiness, while also supporting the development of OWL OS and ARC’s gaming software platform. The company will also expand its team, go-to-market capabilities and strategic partnerships. 
Founded by Jobin Joseph and Kaustubh K. Jadhav, ARC is developing ARC X1, a portable gaming system aimed at making dedicated gaming hardware more accessible to Indian gamers. The company is building its own hardware and software stack, including its proprietary gaming operating system OWL OS. 
ARC X1 is built on an ARM-based architecture powered by Qualcomm technology and is designed to support Android gaming, PC-game compatibility and cloud gaming. 
The company has already crossed 50,000 waitlist sign-ups and has collaborated with Qualcomm ahead of its commercial launch. ARC is also involving gamers in early testing and feedback to refine the product before launch.

title: Groww adds 2.23 lakh active clients in August; Sahi clocks 11% growth
summary:
India’s broking industry added around 5.12 lakh net active clients in August. Groww accounted for nearly 44% of these additions. The market leader added 2.23 lakh active clients during the month, while Sahi recorded the fastest growth among the top 20 brokers.
Groww’s active client base rose from 1.31 crore in July to 1.33 crore in August. Its market share increased from 28.88% to 29.04%.
Zerodha remained the second-largest broker with 67.97 lakh active clients, after a 34,501 clients addition. Angel One retained the third position with 67.19 lakh clients, following an addition of 84,636 users. Their market shares stood at 14.79% and 14.62%, respectively.

Among the top five, ICICI Securities added 23,385 active clients, taking its total to 21.56 lakh, with a 1.10% monthly rise. Upstox added 3,749 users to reach 18.65 lakh, with a 0.20% monthly rise. Their market shares stood at 4.69% and 4.06%, respectively.
Kotak Securities and HDFC Securities ranked sixth and seventh with 13.92 lakh and 13.51 lakh active clients, respectively. Kotak added 9,440 users, while HDFC Securities added 16,198 clients.
Dhan added 19,818 clients, a 1.82% increase, to reach 11.07 lakh and retained the eighth spot. SBI Securities slipped to ninth and recorded a month-on-month decline of 2.46%, losing 26,365 active clients during the month.
Motilal Oswal stood at 10th with 9.06 lakh active clients and 1.97% stake. 
Paytm Money and INDmoney the next two positions with 7.9 lakh and 7.13 lakh clients, respectively. While Paytm Money lost 9,112 users, INDmoney added 7,805 clients during the month.
Sahi was the fastest-growing broker among the top 20, adding 24,718 clients, a 10.83% increase, to reach 2.53 lakh. Its market share stood at 0.55%.
PhonePe’s Share.Market added 5,137 clients, a 2.57% month-on-month increase to reach 2.05 lakh.
The August data highlights the continued concentration of active clients among leading brokers. Groww alone accounted for nearly 44% of the industry’s net additions and widened its market share beyond 29%. The top five brokers collectively control over 67% of the active client base.

title: Blissclub founder’s stake slips below 40% after Series B; Meesho’s Vidit Aatrey holds 6.94%
summary:
D2C athleisure brand BlissClub recently raised Rs 160 crore ($16.8 million) in a Series B round led by Singularity AMC, with Meesho CEO Vidit Aatrey and existing investors Elevation Capital and Eight Roads Ventures also participating. The funding comes amid continued investor interest in India’s D2C apparel and sportswear space.
The fresh capital has pushed BlissClub’s valuation up 62% from its previous round, while the founders’ combined stake has fallen below 40%. Entrackr examined the company’s regulatory filings to decode the latest funding round, cap table, and post-money valuation.
According to the company’s regulatory filings accessed from the Registrar of Companies (RoC), BlissClub’s board approved the issuance of 69,247 Series B compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) at an issue price of Rs 24,503.3 per share to raise Rs 160 crore.
Singularity AMC emerged as the largest investor in the round with an investment of Rs 70 crore, followed by Vidit Aatrey with Rs 50 crore. Existing investors Elevation Capital and Eight Roads Ventures invested Rs 24.66 crore and Rs 15.33 crore, respectively.
According to the company, the fresh capital will be used to expand into new categories, scale its offline retail presence, strengthen product development, and hire talent to support its next phase of growth.
As per Entrackr’s estimates, BlissClub’s valuation surged 62% to around Rs 860 crore (approximately $91 million) following the Series B round, from Rs 532 crore during its Series A round.
Following the latest allotment, Elevation Capital holds a 22.19% stake in the company, followed by Eight Roads Ventures at 14.24%. Singularity AMC, which led the Series B round, holds an 8.14% stake, while Vidit Aatrey owns 6.94%. Co-founder Minu Margeret remains the largest shareholder with a 37.03% stake.


Founded in 2020 by Minu Margeret, BlissClub is a D2C athleisure brand that started with technical activewear for Indian women and has expanded into an omnichannel business with over 40 stores and a recently launched menswear line. Its portfolio spans leggings, tops, outerwear and accessories, sold through its website, marketplaces and retail stores.
BlissClub has yet to file its annual financial report for FY26. In FY25, its operating revenue grew 51.5% to Rs 131.58 crore from Rs 86.88 crore in FY24, while its net loss declined 54.1% to Rs 20.16 crore from Rs 43.92 crore during the same period.
BlissClub competes with several brands in India’s growing women’s activewear and athleisure market, including Kica Active, CAVA Athleisure, Silvertraq, HRX and Cultsport.

title: The fintech infrastructure bet: why the real opportunity was underneath
summary:
My first job out of Berkeley was in enterprise integration, where we connected complex systems like ERP and supply chain platforms, within and across companies, to ultimately deliver a smoother end user experience.
That was where I first understood and appreciated both the importance and, in some ways, the beauty of infrastructure. The end user rarely sees it, but the quality of the experience depends enormously on what sits underneath.
Fast forward to our fintech investing at Better Capital. Soon after developing our neobanking thesis, it became very clear to us that there was an infrastructure layer that was largely independent of the end user experience, but absolutely necessary to enable it.
If India was going to build a new generation of financial services for hundreds of millions of smartphone connected users, someone had to solve the complexity underneath: how fintechs connect with banks, how products get issued and managed, how regulatory requirements are handled, how money moves, and how all of these systems work together reliably.
That led us quite naturally into fintech infrastructure investing.
We started asking a simple question: what is the underlying infrastructure required for all these new financial experiences to exist?
Because whether it was neobanking, new age credit cards, app based lending, investing, wealth management, or many of the experiences that followed, there was almost always a sophisticated infrastructure layer underneath making the product possible.
That thesis has played out quite well.
M2P was one of our earliest investments in the space. It has gone on to power some of the largest fintech experiences in India, expand into multiple markets globally, and continue scaling significantly.
Upswing is another example. It is building the infrastructure behind some of the fastest growing investment and wealth fintechs, enabling products such as fixed deposits, bonds, and other investment experiences to be embedded seamlessly into consumer platforms.
Hyperface has done some remarkable work in cards, building infrastructure that allows brands and financial institutions to launch and operate deeply integrated credit card experiences in a way that was much harder to do earlier.
And these are just a few examples. We have invested in several companies across the financial infrastructure stack over the years.
What the last six or seven years have reinforced for us is that in financial services, some of the most important companies may sit one layer below the consumer experience. The more regulated and operationally complex the product, the more valuable that infrastructure becomes. And perhaps most importantly, we have seen that infrastructure built for the complexity and scale of India can increasingly travel well beyond India.
What continues to excite me is that I don’t think this thesis is anywhere close to being played out.
As financial services become more digital, more embedded, more personalized, and increasingly powered by software and AI, the infrastructure underneath them will become even more important. New consumer experiences will require new infrastructure, and new infrastructure will, in turn, make entirely new experiences possible.
Over the last six or seven years, we have seen the beginnings of that in India. I believe some very large financial infrastructure companies will be built here, and several of them should have the opportunity to power financial experiences well beyond India as well.
That remains one of the areas I am most excited about.
*The second of a five-part series by Vaibhav Domkundwar explores the fintech infrastructure layer powering new financial experiences. Investments in M2P, Upswing, and Hyperface reinforced the thesis that the real opportunity often lies underneath the consumer-facing product. The next three parts will explore other microtrends and lessons.

title: Shiprocket narrows Q1 loss to Rs 13.7 Cr; revenue jumps 34% post IPO
summary:
Logistics and ecommerce enablement platform Shiprocket is showing signs of moving closer to profitability in its first quarterly results after going public.
The company’s consolidated net loss narrowed 24% year-on-year to Rs 13.7 crore in Q1 FY27, compared with Rs 18 crore in the same quarter last year.
Shiprocket’s revenue from operations also rose 33.8% to Rs 592 crore from Rs 442 crore in Q1 FY26, according to the unaudited results filed with the National Stock Exchange (NSE).
According to the investor presentation, the company processed 216 million transactions, with a GMV of Rs 34,662 crore and 2.24 lakh active merchants during Q1 FY27.
Its core business revenue grew 22% year-on-year to Rs 412 crore, while its other emerging businesses saw a 70% growth to Rs 180 crore during the quarter.
On the cost side, the cost of merchant solutions was the largest expenditure at Rs 441 crore, while employee benefits stood at Rs 106 crore. Overall, its total expenditure increased to Rs 619 crore in Q1 FY27 from Rs 474 crore a year earlier.
Meanwhile, Shiprocket’s adjusted EBITDA was positive at Rs 8.9 crore during the quarter, improved from Rs 1 crore in the year-ago period. The company said it remained adjusted EBITDA positive throughout the quarter.
The results come soon after Shiprocket’s stock market debut, making the June quarter an important first test for the company as a listed entity.
The company was trading at Rs 138.49 as of 10:48 AM, giving it a total market capitalisation of Rs 10,076 crore ($1.04 billion).

title: W Health Ventures closes Fund II at Rs 700 Cr
summary:
Healthcare-focused venture firm W Health Ventures (WHV) has closed its second fund at Rs 700 crore, oversubscribing its initial target of Rs 630 crore. 
The fund plans to build 8–10 healthcare companies from the pre-idea stage to category leaders over the next four years.
W Health follows a company-creation model, where its in-house team of physicians, operators and technologists identifies gaps in healthcare delivery and spends 12–18 months evaluating and de-risking an opportunity before bringing in a founding team.
The firm plans to write Rs 30–50 crore cheques and build 2–3 companies every year across India and the US-India corridor.
Fund II has already launched two companies. Everhope Oncology, built with Narayana Health, is focused on coordinated, patient-centric cancer care, while Everbright Health is developing treatments for treatment-resistant depression in the US.
According to W Health Ventures, its portfolio companies have reached 25 million patients to date. The firm said Fund II will focus on solving large, underserved healthcare problems where first-mover solutions can create population-scale impact.
Founded in 2020, W Health Ventures has built companies including Elevate Now, Nivaan, Hoola Health and Everhope Oncology, with offices across Mumbai, Bengaluru, Delhi and Boston.

title: B2B pharma distribution startup Fundly.ai raises $4 Mn led by Accel, Multiply
summary:
Mumbai-based B2B pharma distribution startup Fundly.ai has raised $4 million in a funding round led by existing investors Accel and Multiply Ventures, along with participation from former RBL Bank executive director Rajeev Ahuja and other angel investors. 
The company also raised around $0.9 million in venture debt. 
The fresh capital will be used to expand its digital commerce, payments and credit offerings across India's pharma supply chain. 
Founded in 2021 by Amit Chawla and Shreeram Ramanathan, Fundly.ai initially started as a supply-chain financing platform for pharma businesses. It has since expanded into three areas: B2B commerce, payments and settlement infrastructure, and embedded credit.

title: Udaan to acquire Swiggy-owned Lynk Logistics for Rs 500 Cr
summary:
Foodtech and quick commerce platform Swiggy has agreed to sell its retail distribution business Lynk Logistics to eB2B platform Udaan for Rs 500 crore, in a deal that will expand Udaan’s presence across key consumption markets.
As part of the transaction, Swiggy will receive approximately 2.8% stake in Udaan through preference equity shares issued by Trustroot Internet Pvt Ltd, the parent entity of Udaan. Swiggy will also invest Rs 75 crore in primary equity in Udaan for an additional 0.4% stake.
The transaction comes as Udaan continues to improve its financial performance. Over the 10 quarters from Q4 CY23 to Q1 CY26, its revenue grew at a CAGR of around 25%, while its contribution margin improved by nearly 500 bps and EBITDA burn declined by around 70%. Its private labels now account for 15–25% of Staples sales across operating cities, while Bengaluru, its largest market, has turned EBITDA profitable.
The acquisition will add Lynk’s distribution capabilities, brand relationships and retail network to Udaan’s platform. Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai and Kolkata together contribute around 75% of Lynk’s revenue. The deal will also help Udaan connect leading consumer brands with a wider network of retailers.
Lynk directly or indirectly competes with the likes of Udaan, 1K Kirana Bazaar, Jumbotail, ElasticRun and several other eB2B and retail distribution platforms. These companies serve retailers through technology-led distribution, procurement and supply chain networks, making the acquisition relevant to Udaan’s competitive position in India’s fragmented retail distribution market.
Swiggy had acquired Lynk in July 2023 through a share swap deal, marking its entry into India’s retail B2B distribution market. The transaction value was not disclosed at the time. Lynk, founded in 2015, had a network of more than 100,000 retail stores across eight cities and worked with leading FMCG brands as an authorised distributor.
The latest transaction also follows Udaan’s $160 million recapitalisation, which comprised fresh equity, new debt and debt-to-equity conversion from Lightspeed Venture Partners, M&G Investments and Moonstone Capital. The exercise included around $45 million in private credit financing from a leading global investment management firm and strengthened Udaan’s balance sheet for its next phase of growth.
Swiggy CFO Rahul Bothra said the deal combines Lynk’s capabilities with Udaan’s scale and technology-led platform, while Udaan cofounder and CEO Vaibhav Gupta said the acquisition strengthens the company’s business and expands its presence across important consumption markets.

title: The neobank bet: what backing digital banks in India actually taught us
summary:
With GFF around the corner, I wanted to reflect on what we have actually learned from our fintech portfolio, especially since fintech was the very first area we focused on when we started the fund.
A core part of how we work at Better has been to identify a microtrend early, build conviction in it, and then back multiple companies around that microtrend before it becomes obvious to everyone else. It has served us well over the years.
The very first microtrend we started with was neobanks. In 2018/19 in India, it wasn't really a term yet. My conviction came partly from a vivid memory of a company called Simple from the late 2000s, whose vision was to build a modern digital bank for small businesses. As a small startup founder myself back then, that was something I related to deeply.
By 2018/19 it felt like the ingredients were finally in place in India. A smartphone-first, data-connected, UPI-led population was ready for a genuinely modern banking experience. A number of teams started building around this time and we made several investments: a neobank for Gen Z, one for NRIs, one for SMBs, and a few more.
Soon there was broader conviction in the market and many companies got funded around the same idea. The next several years were about watching them all build and navigate a hard set of constraints.
The hardest one was structural. You cannot easily get a banking license in India, and that single constraint shaped everything. Without a license, delivering a true full-stack customer experience was very hard. Companies had to depend on bank partnerships, and those dependencies caused delays across product, launches and the ability to control the core experience. Compliance and infrastructure constraints added more friction. Consumer and business adoption was genuinely strong, but the path to the fuller vision kept hitting the same ceiling.
Slice was the one that broke through it. By acquiring a bank and becoming a full-stack neobank, it unlocked the vision many of us had held on to for years. Today, Slice is one of the top credit card issuers in the country within about a year of going full-stack, ahead of many large banks, and posted a PAT of around ₹46 crore in Q1FY27.
And Slice is not the only story here. Several others from this cohort are still very much in play, and they have delivered genuinely incredible improvements in customer experience along the way. I am excited to see how they navigate the next chapter and unlock more of the vision we all started with.
This is exactly why we invest the way we do. Get the microtrend right, back multiple shots at it early, and stay long enough for the category to be redefined. Neobanks were our first real proof of that.
 
*This is the first of a five-part series by Vaibhav Domkundwar on the microtrends that have shaped his investment journey. Neobanks were the starting point, and the experience reinforced a simple thesis: identify a shift early, back the right founders, and stay patient as a category evolves. The next three parts will explore the other microtrends and the lessons they offered.

summary:

The latest commitment takes the total capital committed by GMC to $50 million, including the $10 million invested in 2025. The capital will be deployed over the next 30 months through a mix of debt, quasi-equity and equity.
HerSpace will use the funds to expand its affordable employee housing offerings across key manufacturing hubs, including Greater Bengaluru, Hosur, Chennai and Andhra Pradesh. The company will also invest in people and systems to support its growth.
Founded in 2023 by Bob Pattillo and Puneeth Thimmegowda, HerSpace provides leased accommodation for industrial workers. The startup funds, designs, builds and operates workforce housing facilities, with statutory compliance incorporated into its operations.
The company currently has more than 950 modular beds delivered and operational, while over 10,000 beds are in the pipeline.
“This funding milestone marks a defining moment for HerSpace and reflects the immense market opportunity ahead, as well as the dedication of our talented team including our founders Mr. Bob Pattillo and Mr. Puneeth Thimmegowda,” said Simha Nagaraj, CEO of HerSpace Manufacturing.
HerSpace’s expansion comes amid growing focus on worker accommodation as a factor supporting India’s manufacturing sector. A 2024 NITI Aayog report highlighted inadequate housing near industrial hubs as a constraint for worker migration, retention and productivity, particularly for women workers.
HerSpace said its accommodation model can also help employers reduce employee transport costs and their carbon footprint.

title: Exclusive: DaMENSCH raises fresh funding at flat valuation of Rs 600 Cr
summary:
DaMENSCH has raised fresh capital from existing backer A91 Partners and new investor Tancom Electronics, but the latest round has not moved its valuation. The flat pricing comes as the direct to consumer men’s apparel market enters a more competitive phase, with brands now under pressure to turn topline growth into profitability.
In May 2024, the company had raised Rs 21.62 crore (approximately $2.5 million) in its extended Series B round from existing investors.
The board at DaMENSCH has approved the allotment of 887 compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) at an issue price of Rs 1,69,052 per share to raise Rs 15 crore from A91 Partners, according to the company’s regulatory filing accessed through the Registrar of Companies.
Separately, the company issued 168 CCPS at an issue price of Rs 1,42,692 per share to raise Rs 2.40 crore from Tancom Electronics. Together, the two tranches helped DaMENSCH raise Rs 17.40 crore in this round.
As per Entrackr’s estimates, DaMENSCH’s valuation is flat to Rs 600 crore ($63.5 million at current exchange rate) from its previous valuation of $70-75 million or Rs 582 crore . 
The company plans to use the fresh capital to meet its business requirements and support its growth, as per filings.
Founded in 2018 by Anurag Saboo and Gaurav Pushkar, DaMENSCH is a D2C men’s fashion and lifestyle brand that offers innerwear, casualwear, and everyday apparel products via its own platform and marketplaces.
DaMENSCH has raised over $28 million to date, including its $16.6 million Series B round led by A91 Partners in February 2022.
A91 Partners remains the largest shareholder in the company with a 22.45% stake, followed by Matrix with 12.76%. Saama Capital and Whiteboard Capital hold 11.14% and 9.61%, respectively. The company’s co-founders, Gaurav Pushkar and Anurag Saboo, hold 10.87% each.


DaMENSCH is yet to file its FY26 results, but its FY25 performance shows how competition is shaping up in D2C men’s apparel. Its revenue grew 34% to Rs 118 crore, while XYXX scaled 46% to Rs 187 crore and narrowed its loss to Rs 25.5 crore. Bummer remained smaller, with revenue up 22% to Rs 11 crore, but losses doubled. 
The numbers point to a market where brands are scaling, but the gap is emerging in how efficiently they convert growth into profitability. As competition intensifies, scale, repeat purchases and distribution economics will become increasingly important for these firms.

title: Voice AI startup Navana.ai raises Rs 40 Cr led by Ronnie Screwvala
summary:
Voice AI startup Navana.ai has raised Rs 40 crore ($4.2 million) in a Series A round led by entrepreneur and investor Ronnie Screwvala. The round also saw participation from Antler India, Sharad Sanghi, Sandeep Singhal, Paula Mariwala and other investors.
The company plans to deploy the fresh capital to expand its Voice AI deployments among BFSI enterprises, strengthen its speech models for Indian languages and dialects, and develop its AI Contact Centre and automated evaluation platform.
Founded by brothers Raoul and Jai Nanavati, Navana.ai provides voice AI solutions to regulated enterprises, with a focus on data privacy and compliance through on-premise deployments. The startup claims to have processed more than 100 million voice AI minutes for BFSI companies including Bajaj Finserv, Protean, Ujjivan Small Finance Bank, Jana Small Finance Bank and Grihum Housing Finance.
Navana.ai has developed proprietary speech models covering 12 Indian languages and 45 dialects. Its models are designed to handle challenges such as background noise, overlapping speech, code switching and regional accents. The company has also collaborated with IISc Bengaluru, IIT Madras, Microsoft Research and the Gates Foundation.
The startup said its Bodhi speech model achieved the highest accuracy in a benchmarking exercise conducted across Indian voice AI platforms using real world speech samples.
Ronnie Screwvala said that Navana.ai is addressing the linguistic complexity of India and that voice AI could become a critical part of the country’s digital infrastructure. He also highlighted data localisation and regulatory compliance as key considerations for enterprise adoption.
Navana.ai is building voice AI infrastructure for regulated industries, with its Bodhi speech models being used by BFSI companies to serve customers in their own languages at scale.

title: Exclusive: Swish to raise around $24 Mn at $175 Mn valuation
summary:
Swish is raising fresh capital from Bertelsmann India Investments, adding a new institutional investor to its captable. The round comes just months after its last fundraise, pointing to continued investor interest in the emerging 10-minute food delivery model.
The Bengaluru-based startup is raising Rs 224.54 crore (around $24 million) in an extended Series B round led by Bertelsmann India, with the participation from its existing investors.
This will be the company’s second funding round this year. In March, Swish raised $38 million in a round led by Hara Global and Bain Capital.
The board at Swish has passed a special resolution to issue 4,123 Series B2 compulsory convertible preference shares at an issue price of Rs 5,44,616 each to raise the above mentioned amount, its regulatory filing accessed from the Registrar of Companies shows.
Bertelsmann India Investments will lead the round with an investment of Rs 143.34 crore ($15 million), joining Swish’s captable. Bain Capital Ventures will invest Rs 62 crore ($6.5 million), while Accel and Hara Global will participate with Rs 14.32 crore and Rs 4.8 crore, respectively.
According to the Entrackr’s estimates, Swish’s valuation will surge over 30% to Rs 1,653 crore or around $175 million post-money, from Rs 1,268 crore in its previous $38 million round.
Following the allotment of the new round, Bertelsmann India Investments will acquire an 8.67% stake in Swish. Accel will remain the largest shareholder with a 23.48% stake, followed by Hara Global with 17.93% and Bain Capital Ventures with 9.97%. Its co-founders Aniket Shah, Sureshkumar Saran and Ujjwal Sukheja will retain 10.98% each.
In June, Moneycontrol reported that Swish was in talks to raise $20 million from Bertelsmann India Investments. 
Founded in 2024, Swish operates a 10 minute food delivery model through a network of cloud kitchens located close to demand clusters. The company focuses on delivering meals within a limited radius to enable faster turnaround times. 
Prior to this round, the firm had raised around $54 million, including a $14 million round in March 2025, which was exclusively reported by Entrackr.
Launched in July 2024, Swish reported Rs 4 crore in revenue and a total loss of Rs 19 crore during the eight-month period of FY25. The company is yet to file its FY26 financial results.
Swish operates in a market that is no longer short of well-funded competitors. Blinkit’s Bistro, Zepto Cafe and Swiggy’s Bolt are already testing different approaches to faster food delivery, while cloud-kitchen players such as Rebel Foods and Curefoods add another layer of competition.
For Swish, the challenge will be to build enough order density and repeat demand to make its focused model work better than larger platforms with deeper distribution and existing consumer traffic.

title: Pet food and nutrition brand Lickicious raises Rs 19 Cr led by Prath Ventures
summary:
Pet food and nutrition brand Lickicious raises Rs 19 Cr to scale manufacturing and expand categories
Pet food and nutrition brand Lickicious has raised Rs 19 crore in growth capital through a mix of equity and institutional debt as it looks to scale its annual revenue to Rs 100 crore.
Prath Ventures led the institutional backing in the round, while the founders of Atomberg and several senior industry CXOs are also among the company’s early backers.
Founded in 2024 by Shashwat Sahai and Chandan Jha, Lickicious is operated by Nuvexo Wellness Pvt Ltd and sells food and nutrition products for dogs and cats.
The fresh capital will be deployed across three areas: capacity, capability and category expansion. The company is developing a 60,000 sq ft manufacturing and distribution footprint to increase production capacity, improve supply reliability and strengthen control over product quality.
Lickicious will also invest in research and development, quality, manufacturing, supply chain, brand and commercial functions. It plans to expand its portfolio across products, formats, species and sales channels, moving beyond its digital first model towards an omnichannel pet nutrition business.
The company is targeting Rs 100 crore in annual revenue as an important milestone, while aiming to become one of India’s top three pet food companies over the next decade.
“Our next phase is about building better products, stronger manufacturing and a stronger brand,” said Shashwat Sahai, cofounder of Nuvexo Wellness.
Prath Ventures Managing Partner Harmanpreet Singh said India’s pet food market is becoming increasingly product and trust led. He added that Lickicious is investing in manufacturing, product development, category and channel expansion to support its next phase of growth.
The company focuses on palatability, transparent nutrition and quality across its pet food and nutrition products for dogs and cats.

title: Spactech startup Pixxel raises $100 Mn in Series C led by Temasek, Seraphim
summary:
Bengaluru-based space-tech startup Pixxel has raised $100 million in its Series C funding round co-led by Temasek and Seraphim Space.
The round also saw participation from new investors 360 ONE Asset and IMM Investment, along with existing backers Radical Ventures and growX Ventures, among others. The latest fundraise takes Pixxel’s total funding to $195 million. The company said the round is the largest funding raised by a space-tech company in India.
Media reports suggest that Pixxel is being valued at around $450-500 million in the latest round.
Pixxel will use the fresh capital to expand beyond hyperspectral imaging into advanced sensing satellites, Earth intelligence software, sovereign space systems and satellite manufacturing. Its plans include expanding the Honeybee constellation, developing high-resolution optical imaging satellites, scaling its Aurora Earth intelligence platform and increasing manufacturing capacity through Gigapixxel.
Founded by Awais Ahmed and Kshitij Khandelwal, Pixxel initially focused on hyperspectral imaging satellites and has since expanded into Earth intelligence software and satellite systems for commercial and sovereign missions.
Before the latest round, Pixxel had raised $95 million from investors including Google, Lightspeed, Radical Ventures, Blume Ventures, growX Ventures, Glade Brook Partners and Seraphim. The startup closed its Series B round at $60 million in December 2024.
The latest round comes shortly after Skyroot Aerospace became the first Indian space-tech startup to achieve unicorn status, crossing the $1 billion valuation mark.
Over the past two years, Pixxel has deployed six Firefly satellites, launched Aurora and secured contracts with NASA and the NRO. It has also won multiple iDEX challenges from the Ministry of Defence and was selected to lead the development of India’s first public-private Earth observation constellation of 12 satellites under IN-SPACe.

title: Ola Electric approves Rs 1,500 Cr fundraise; COO Hyun Shik Park resigns
summary:
Electric two-wheeler maker Ola Electric has approved a plan to raise up to Rs 1,500 crore through the issuance of equity shares or convertible securities.
The company’s board approved the proposal on September 5. The fundraise can be carried out through a further public offer, rights issue, QIP, private placement or other permitted routes, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.
The development comes just three months after Ola raised Rs 780 crore through a QIP in June, when it allotted around 21.76 crore shares at Rs 35.86 apiece to qualified institutional buyers.
Meanwhile, Ola Electric COO Hyun Shik Park has resigned, effective from the closing business hours of September 5. The company said Park resigned from his role as a Senior Management Personnel due to personal reasons.
The fresh fundraise comes at a difficult time for the EV two-wheeler maker, which has been dealing with falling market share, customer complaints and a decline in its share price and market capitalisation.
In Q1 FY27, Ola Electric’s revenue from operations fell 45% YoY to Rs 455 crore, while its net loss narrowed to Rs 336 crore from Rs 428 crore a year earlier. The company recorded 13,170 vehicle registrations in July, giving it a 6.8% market share.
Ola Electric has also been scaling up its battery-cell manufacturing operations. It recently secured Rs 95.81 crore under the government’s PLI-Auto scheme for FY27.
The board has also approved increasing the company’s authorised share capital from Rs 8,318.5 crore to Rs 8,721.9 crore, subject to shareholder approval.

Rentomojo’s upcoming IPO is set to generate multi-fold returns for several of its early investors, with one shareholder set to clock a 152X return on its investment, while existing shareholders are looking to offload shares worth Rs 1,106 crore through the OFS.
According to Entrackr’s analysis, at the upper price band of Rs 404 per share, Accel India is set to generate around 8.63X returns on its Rs 317 crore OFS. Madison India could clock around 7.22X on its Rs 96.9 crore share sale, while ValueQuest and Edelweiss are expected to earn around 5.4X on their respective OFS shares worth Rs 109.6 crore and Rs 116.5 crore.
Chiratae Ventures is likely to generate around 4.93X returns on its Rs 194.1 crore OFS, while GMO could earn around 4.24X on its Rs 95.1 crore share sale.

Among individual shareholders, Nitish Mittersain, founder of Nazara Technologies, is set to emerge as one of the biggest beneficiaries. Mittersain’s investment in Rentomojo was his first startup investment. He is selling shares worth around Rs 6 crore through the OFS, which could fetch him around 152X returns based on the acquisition cost disclosed in the company’s offer documents and the upper IPO price band of Rs 404 per share.
Rajeev Chitrabhanu HUF is another notable early shareholder, with its Rs 12.4 crore OFS potentially generating around 26.6X returns.
The company’s founder Geetansh Bamania is set to offload shares worth Rs 34.3 crore, while other OFS participants include Japan-based Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Venture Capital (MSIVC), Pratithi Investment Trust, Renaud Laplanche and others.
The returns are based on the weighted average acquisition cost disclosed in Rentomojo’s offer documents and the upper IPO price band of Rs 404 per share. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of Rs 150 crore and an OFS of around Rs 1,105.6 crore, giving the company a valuation of around Rs 4,200 crore at the upper band.
Rentomojo’s IPO is scheduled to open for subscription on September 9 and close on September 11.
Financially, Rentomojo has continued to grow while remaining profitable. Its revenue from operations rose 45.5% year-on-year to Rs 387 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 266 crore in FY25. Profit after tax jumped 142% to Rs 104.2 crore from Rs 43.1 crore in the previous fiscal.

title: Funding and acquisitions in Indian startups this week [Aug 31 - Sep 05]
summary:
This week, 25 Indian startups raised $303.7 million across five growth-stage deals, 16 early-stage deals and three undisclosed rounds. The week also saw seven key hires, four mergers and acquisitions, two startup shutdowns and 250 layoffs.

In contrast, 24 startups had collectively secured about $218.7 million in the previous week.
[Growth-stage deals]
Growth-stage startups raised $201.9 million across five deals this week. Digital banking startup Slice led the funding with a $100 million round at a $450 million valuation, led by Neo Wealth with participation from Kado Global, Moore Strategic Ventures and Raise Financial.
Wearable tech startup Ultrahuman has raised $70 million in a round led by Qualcomm Ventures, with participation from Labcorp, Alpha Wave, Blume Ventures, Nexus Venture Partners, Alteria and other investors. D2C skincare brand SUGAR Cosmetics has raised Rs 144.5 crore ($15.2 million) from existing investor A91 Partners at a valuation of Rs 755 crore, down 75% from its last valuation of Rs 3,000 crore.
Homegrown sneaker brand Comet has raised around Rs 100 crore in its Series B round led by Belgium-based investment firm Verlinvest. Pune-based deeptech company Aeron Systems has raised Rs 45 crore ($4.7 million) in a Pre-Series B funding round
[Early-stage deals]
Early-stage startups raised $101.8 million across 16 deals this week. BaaS provider Yuma Energy raised $35 million in Series A funding led by Magna International, while NextGen Finance raised Rs 215 crore led by Beams Fintech Fund.
Consumer health startup Cradlewise raised $12 million in Series A funding led by 3one4 Capital and Prudent Investment Management. Space infrastructure startup Kepler Aerospace raised $8 million in seed funding led by Blue Ashva Capital.
Former Google AI lead Prashant Jalan launched Guickly with $4.2 million in seed funding led by Engineering Capital. Deeptech startup Zenergize Technologies also raised $4 million in Pre-Series A funding led by Giraffe Studios.
Other startups that raised funding this week included deeptech firms Zenergize Technologies, Minimac Systems and Alteon, along with indoor air-quality company YOGa Clean Air and six other startups. 
Voice-first AI tutoring platform YoLearn.ai, English learning app SpeakX, neurotechnology startup Neurotech and deeptech firm BQP also raised funding this week, with amounts undisclosed.
[City and segment-wise deals]
Bengaluru led the funding charts with 14 startup deals during the week, followed by Delhi-NCR with five. Mumbai, Pune and Hyderabad also recorded deals.

Deeptech startups led the sectors with five deals, followed by healthtech and AI with four deals each. E-commerce bagged 3 deals during the week while Fintech and edtech startups recorded two deals each, while e-commerce, EV, spacetech, manufacturing and other sectors also saw funding activity.
[Series-wise deals]
Series A rounds led the week with 8 deals, followed by Series A and pre-seed rounds with five  deals and four deals respectively. Series D, Series B, Pre-Series A, Series C  and pre-Series B also recorded one deal each during the week.

[Week-on-week funding trend]
On a weekly basis, startup funding surged over 39% to $303.7 million from $218.7 million raised in the previous week.
The average weekly funding over the past eight weeks stood at around $218.25 million across 20 deals.
[Key Hirings / Departures]
This week, Bengaluru-based digital healthcare platform MediBuddy appointed Shalabh Shrivastava as its Head of Operations to strengthen processes and technology-led execution. Fintech platform Pine Labs also appointed Jayaram Karthik, former SVP of Business Operations at Razorpay, as its chief operations officer.
Wingify has appointed Mehernaz Dalal as its chief financial officer. Boldfit has appointed former Lenskart chief business officer Oliver Kaye as its chief operating officer. Enterprise SaaS company Genefied has appointed Neha Lakhwara as Head of Investor Relations and Strategy. Technology-led credit inclusion platform BankSathi has appointed Nitish Kumar Bugalia as co-founder and chief operating officer.
[Mergers and Acquisitions]
Gurugram-based insurtech startups InsuranceDekho and RenewBuy have merged to create a unified pan-India insurance distribution platform under the InsuranceDekho brand, with founder and CEO Ankit Agrawal leading the combined entity. 
Bengaluru-based travel-fintech platform Niyo has agreed to acquire Capital India Finance’s forex and cross-border business, operated under the RemitX brand. The deal will bring RemitX’s branch network, distribution partners, employees and brand under Niyo.
Adobe has picked up India based marketing intelligence startup Rilo in a deal involving the licensing of its technology and acquisition of its team. This is Adobe’s second acquisition from India.
Cloud-based lending platform Lenra AI has acquired Israel-based data science company Data Harbor in an undisclosed deal. Founded by Ephraim Goldin, Data Harbor provides real-time data consolidation, predictive analytics and data science services, with the acquisition aimed at strengthening Lenra’s Intelligence Stack and automation across the lending lifecycle.
[Layoffs]
Uber is set to lay off around 200-250 employees in India as part of a global restructuring, with cuts expected across its People and Earners teams, according to an ET report. Globally, the company is eliminating around 3,300 roles, or 10% of its workforce, in its largest workforce reduction since the Covid-19 pandemic.
Eternal, the parent company of Zomato and Blinkit, is set to lay off around 250 employees as part of a restructuring of its customer support operations.
[Shutdown]
Gurugram-based e-grocery startup Satvacart has shut down after 12 years, with August 28 marking its last day of operations. The shutdown follows years of funding challenges, with smaller capital tranches proving insufficient to rebuild and scale the business.

UPI processed an average 791 million transactions worth Rs 96,205 crore daily during the month.

The move follows a year of learnings since CREW’s launch, with travel emerging as the category seeing the strongest demand for seamless, end-to-end convenience.

Unacademy cofounder and CEO Gaurav Munjal confirmed the deal, noting that the company had raised funds at its peak but is now being sold at a fraction of that valuation.

title: Sugar Cosmetics raises Rs 144 Cr at Rs 755 Cr valuation; early investors seek steep discount exits
summary:
Sugar Cosmetics, once among the better-known names in India’s D2C beauty wave, has raised Rs 144.5 crore from existing investor A91 Partners as the company faces continued pressure on revenue and profitability. The funding comes alongside efforts by some early investors to find buyers for their stakes at steep discounts to the company’s peak valuation.
The board approved the allotment of 1,12,248 Series CCPS at an issue price of Rs 12,871 per share to raise Rs 144.5 crore, according to regulatory filings. A91 Partners subscribed to the entire issue.
Based on the allotment and resulting shareholding, Entrackr estimates that the transaction values Sugar at around Rs 755 crore post-money, 75% below its peak valuation of around Rs 3,000 crore. A91 will hold around 19.97% in the company following the new round.
On Friday, ET reported that the firm was raising Rs 140-150 crore from A91 at a valuation of Rs 500-600 crore. 
The latest primary round is also taking place as some existing investors explore secondary exits. Sources said investors are looking to sell stakes worth up to Rs 150 crore. Some early backers have been approaching potential buyers at steep discounts to Sugar’s peak valuation.
Entrackr has also learnt that a consulting firm has been pitching Sugar shares at a fraction of its peak valuation, with a minimum transaction size of around Rs 25 crore. The discussions underline the extent of the valuation correction since the peak of the D2C funding cycle.
Sugar was valued at around $400 million, or roughly Rs 3,000 crore, in 2022 when it raised $50 million in a Series D round led by L Catterton. At the time, the company was expanding its offline retail footprint and had emerged as a prominent youth-focused cosmetics brand.
The business has since lost momentum. Sugar’s revenue declined 20% to Rs 404 crore in FY25 from Rs 505 crore in FY24, while its net loss almost doubled to Rs 135 crore from Rs 68 crore. 
Founded by Vineeta Singh and Kaushik Mukherjee, Sugar started as an online-first beauty brand before building a sizable offline presence. It sells makeup and personal care products through marketplaces, its own platform and a network of retail outlets.
The latest round paints a very different picture from Sugar’s 2022 fundraise. A91, which already held roughly a fifth of Sugar, is putting fresh capital into the company even as other investors look for exits at sharply lower valuations.
For Sugar, the funding provides capital to stabilise the business, but also marks a clear reset in investor expectations. It now needs to rebuild revenue, improve profitability and demonstrate stronger unit economics.
The reset, however, does not necessarily spell the end of Sugar’s growth story. Its brand recognition and distribution network give it room to recover if it can sharpen its product portfolio, improve economics and return to growth.
For early investors, the priority appears to have shifted from waiting for a large exit to finding liquidity at a fraction of Sugar’s earlier valuation. The latest round reflects how sharply expectations have changed, while leaving Sugar with the task of proving it can bounce back.

title: D2C sneaker brand Comet raises Rs 100 Cr in Series B led by Verlinvest
summary:
Homegrown sneaker brand Comet has raised around Rs 100 crore in its Series B round led by Belgium-based investment firm Verlinvest, as it looks to expand its retail footprint and strengthen its product and technology capabilities.
Existing investors Elevation Capital and Nexus Venture Partners also participated in the round. Angel investors including Urban Company cofounder Abhiraj Singh Bhal, Snap’s global chief business officer Ajit Mohan and Bhaane founder Anand Ahuja also joined the round.
On Wednesday, Entrackr exclusively reported that Comet was raising fresh capital. As per our estimates, the funding values Comet at around Rs 535 crore, a more than threefold jump from its post-money valuation of around Rs 167 crore after its Series A round in 2024.
Comet plans to use the fresh capital to accelerate retail expansion, product development and technology capabilities, along with investments in research and development. The company is also developing its own sole moulds and tooling for new footwear models.
Founded in 2023 by Utkarsh Gupta and Dishant Daryani, Bengaluru-based Comet currently has four footwear models and plans to double its portfolio to eight models by the end of next year. It is also preparing to launch a women-focused model backed by dedicated sole tooling.
The company has grown its revenue ninefold since its previous institutional fundraise and is set to reach 10 stores this month. It plans to expand its retail network to 20 stores by the end of FY27.
In FY25, Comet’s revenue rose nearly fourfold to Rs 29 crore, while its loss widened to Rs 4.39 crore. The company is yet to file its FY26 financials.
Comet is among a growing set of homegrown sneaker brands, alongside Gully Labs, Neeman’s, ARCs and Doc Sneakers.

title: "I Shut Down Satvacart 45 Days Before Break-Even"
summary:
Orders had risen 2.5 times in two days and the contribution margin was positive. But the bank account was empty, investors had walked away and, after 12 years of absorbing every shock, I could absorb no more. A founder’s capacity is capital too
On August 28, 2026, I shut down Satvacart.
The decision came at a strange moment. Orders had risen 2.5 times in two days. The contribution margin was positive. Our calculations suggested we were roughly 45 days from break-even. After 12 years of rebuilding the company through funding droughts, operational breakdowns and multiple changes of model, the business was moving in the right direction.
I was not.
Our funds were at zero. Rain and waterlogging had disrupted deliveries. A delivery executive stopped reporting because his salary was unpaid, forcing us to use Porter. A $500,000 funding conversation had already collapsed. Then, on August 27, an investor considering a larger $3 million cheque backed out. The following day, our operations head called: a picker would not work beyond noon. Operations would have to stop.
None of these problems was new. I had solved some versions of each many times. On 11 occasions in 12 years, I had virtually no money in my pocket and none in the company’s bank account. Salaries had been delayed. Operations had stalled. Once, the situation escalated until I had to call the police. Each time, we found a way through.
This time, I could not find a responsible reason to ask employees to work unpaid for a few more days while I chased another investor for another small cheque. Satvacart did not close because customers had disappeared or because online grocery had become impossible. It closed because its founder had reached saturation.
That distinction matters. Startups measure runway in months of cash. They rarely measure how many shocks the founder can still absorb. Founder capacity is capital too, and mine had run out.
The business had not run out of juice
Satvacart began 12 years ago as one of Gurugram’s early online grocery businesses. We survived several funding meltdowns, rebuilt the company five times and demonstrated profitability at one stage. Transactions were still growing when I stopped.
Gurugram has roughly 10 lakh households and continues to grow rapidly. Even without meaningful marketing, we were seeing around 300 app launches and four first transactions a day. Our average order value was ₹950. Some loyal customers placed 15 to 30 orders a month. Our contribution margin had previously reached about ₹250 an order.
The plan was simple enough to fit on a napkin. Get back to 2,500 households, lift average frequency from four orders a month to seven and hold contribution margin at ₹250 an order. That would produce ₹43.75 lakh in monthly contribution margin. After roughly ₹10 lakh in fixed cluster costs, including marketing, one cluster could generate about ₹33.75 lakh in monthly EBIT.
Then replicate the cluster. Internal cash generation, not endless fundraising, would finance expansion. The dot-com crash, the Lehman crisis and Covid had all delivered the same warning: external capital can disappear overnight.
The model was not fantasy. We had made it profitable before. What we never completed was the replication. In grocery, a profitable store is evidence; a profitable network is the company. We proved the first and ran out of capital and founder capacity before proving the second.
What 12 years taught me about capital
My first fundraising mistake was almost comical. I told an investor I needed ₹25 lakh because that was what my spreadsheet said would take us to profitability. I had budgeted for the plan, not for reality. The seed round eventually became ₹86 lakh.
A founder should not raise enough for everything to go right. The money must cover suppliers, salaries, technology, experiments, failed campaigns, delayed fundraising and the things nobody had the imagination to predict. Once a business has paying customers, I now believe a seed round of around $2 million is often the minimum required to reach the next independently fundable milestone. Anything smaller can leave the company perpetually fundraising and dangerously distracted.
More money, however, is not permission to become careless. We developed a small ritual: no payments for 48 hours after investor funds hit the bank. The pause prevented the psychological release of finally seeing money from turning into instant spending.
Undercapitalisation also distorts behaviour. Towards the end, we were raising ₹7 lakh, ₹2 lakh, ₹3 lakh and ₹5 lakh at a time, sometimes through deeply discounted rounds. Satvacart had more than 125 shareholders and another 340 CSOP subscribers through Tyke. If half the shareholders had put in ₹2 lakh each, we could have raised about ₹1.25 crore, enough to take the business to profitability. Most had stopped answering calls and messages. A few continued to help, but cheques of ₹50,000 or ₹1 lakh bought days, not a future.
Small cheques can keep a company alive while quietly preventing it from confronting whether it has a fundable path. Survival and progress are not the same thing.
Growth can lie
The grocery business taught me to distrust growth when it is separated from unit economics.
Take a ₹10 packet of Parle-G to a neighbourhood kirana and offer the shopkeeper ₹5. He will refuse because he understands the transaction immediately: selling a ₹10 product for ₹5 destroys value. A startup can sell the same packet for ₹2.50, classify the ₹7.50 loss as customer acquisition cost and celebrate the resulting spike in orders.
It has acquired a transaction. It may not have acquired a customer.
The distortion gets worse when companies showcase Net Order Value calculated using MRP multiplied by units sold instead of the price customers actually paid. A deeper discount can then create prettier growth. Activity rises, headlines improve and capital is raised, while the underlying economics deteriorate.
At Satvacart, contribution margin became the number I trusted. Revenue and orders matter only after a founder knows what each additional transaction contributes. Discounts can introduce a customer to a service. They cannot be the service.
Customer obsession also requires visibility, not slogans. In 2016, we built a simple post-delivery feedback system that allowed customers to write whatever they wanted. Nearly 90 per cent of our customers had my phone number, and I called many of them directly. The team knew poor service could reach me without travelling through layers of hierarchy.
Founders often treat systems as automation. The first job of a system is more basic: tell you that something is going wrong before it becomes a crisis. Capital can buy software and staff. It cannot compensate for a management team that has become blind to the doorstep.
Reduce the problem before expanding the dream
The most useful advice I received rarely sounded grand. Early on, I spent weeks trying to perfect the company’s name. Vijay, a friend and adviser, recognised the analysis paralysis and pushed me to launch. Years later, when others thought Satvacart should close, he came to the office and asked: ‘Do you want to survive, or do you want to shut down?’
I said I wanted to survive. He told me to surrender the office, remove non-essential staff and protect only the core operation.
Another adviser, Ujj Nath, shared the story of Subway narrowing its focus to one store when bankruptcy threatened. One store has fewer problems than 100. Make it work, understand why it works and only then multiply it.
Startup culture often mistakes a wider battlefield for greater ambition. Sometimes ambition means reducing the problem until it can be solved. Satvacart’s cluster plan came from that lesson. It was our attempt to turn one viable operating unit into a repeatable company.
The company must sometimes leave the founder’s head
The question that stalked me for 12 years was painfully simple: Kya hoga, kaise hoga? What will happen, and how will it happen?
No founder can answer it honestly every night. My former boss Rahul Rishi, a partner at EY, once told me that problems eventually get resolved if you keep trying. I learnt that the situation at 11 pm is not necessarily the situation at 11 am. Make one more call. Solve the next problem. Stay alive long enough for circumstances to change.
Spirituality helped me live with what could not be solved that night. The lesson I took from the Bhagavad Gita was to work on the duty in front of me without pretending I controlled the future. Glenn Harrold’s deep-sleep recordings helped quieten the loops of overthinking. Neither is a prescription. Every founder needs a method that allows the company to leave the head for a few hours. Without one, the business consumes the person expected to save it.
In Satvacart’s final days, we even built what I called an AI-led marketing organisation. ChatGPT acted as CMO, Codex as analyst and executor, Gemini worked on Google Ads and Meta AI on Facebook campaigns. I made the final decisions. Orders jumped 2.5 times in two days while contribution margin stayed positive.
The machine was working. The founder was exhausted.
Closing Satvacart does not persuade me that online grocery has room for only two giants. It persuades me that a viable grocery company still needs sufficient capital, disciplined economics, systems that expose trouble early and a founder able to survive the distance between proof and scale.
We had customers. We had positive contribution. We had a route to break-even. What we no longer had was enough cash or human capacity to travel the final 45 days.
That is the hardest lesson I carry from Satvacart: a startup can remain alive on a spreadsheet after the person carrying it has reached the end.
By our guest author Rahul H. Saxena.
Rahul H. Saxena was the founder and CEO of Satvacart, an online grocery startup he built and ran for 12 years until its operations were discontinued in August 2026. Before founding Satvacart, he worked as a consultant at EY and held corporate strategy roles at Cleartrip, with experience spanning strategy, business transformation, data analytics and systems design. He also worked with O3 Capital and NetApp.

title: Cars24 revenue declines for second year in a row, core biz falls 23% in FY26
summary:
Cars24’s revenue continued to decline for the second consecutive year as the used-car marketplace navigated a challenging FY26 marked by cost cuts, layoffs and a series of senior-level exits.
The company’s revenue from operations fell 18.3% to Rs 5,092 crore in the fiscal year ended March 2026, from Rs 6,233 crore in FY25 and Rs 6,917 crore in FY24, according to its consolidated financial statements filed with the Registrar of Companies (RoC).

The sale of cars through its auction and retail businesses remained the biggest contributor, accounting for around 87% of operating revenue. However, revenue from this segment declined 22.7% to Rs 4,349 crore in FY26, pointing to stress in its core used-car business. The segment had already declined 11% in FY25, indicating that pressure on the core biz has persisted for a second consecutive year and weighed on overall scale.
The remaining operating income came from financial services, including interest on loans provided through its Loans24 platform, as well as service fees, parking fees, and other offerings such as insurance assistance and warranties. These collectively contributed around Rs 653 crore during the year.
Cars24 also recorded Rs 128 crore in other income, largely from interest on current deposits, taking its total income to Rs 5,220 crore, compared with Rs 6,358 crore in the previous fiscal year.
With the business shrinking, car procurement remained the company’s largest cost centre but fell 23.7% to Rs 4,212 crore. However, employee benefit expenses rose 33.4% to Rs 806 crore, while marketing expenses remained broadly stable at Rs 105 crore. In the end, Cars24’s overall expenses declined 17.7% to Rs 5,674 crore during the last fiscal year.
The company’s financial year also saw significant organisational changes. In April 2025, Cars24 laid off around 200 employees across functions as part of a restructuring exercise, with CEO Vikram Chopra saying some projects and roles had been added prematurely.
The leadership churn continued in 2026. India used-car CEO Himanshu Ratnoo stepped down in March, with Chopra taking direct oversight of the business. Co-founder Gajendra Jangid subsequently stepped back from day-to-day operations, while co-founder and COO Mehul Agrawal also exited his operating role in April.
Despite the decline in revenue, Cars24 narrowed its net loss by 18.8% to Rs 441 crore in FY26 from Rs 543 crore in FY25. Its EBITDA margin stood at 8.63%, while ROCE was 19.6% during the last fiscal year.
Spinny has emerged as the leading player in India’s used-car retail space, with revenue growing over 28% in FY26, unlike Cars24, which saw another year of decline. Spinny touched the Rs 6,000 crore revenue threshold in FY26 and is expected to grow 25-30% in FY27, according to sources. The company also raised $320 million over the past year, giving it more room to scale as Cars24 works to regain momentum.
For Cars24, the immediate priority is to restore growth in its used-car business before pursuing larger expansion plans. The company is also yet to complete its reverse flip from Singapore to India, adding another step before it can seriously prepare for a public listing.
With the IPO timeline no longer clearly in sight, Cars24 will need to demonstrate that its used-car retail and auction businesses can return to growth and support stronger economics. Until then, narrowing losses alone may not be enough to rebuild the scale and market confidence needed for a successful public-market push.

The higher basket size could give Minutes an edge as it scales its quick commerce operations. While the platform initially had a higher mix of mobile orders, electronics and mobile categories have become a bigger contributor to its overall portfolio over the past year.
Flipkart’s expertise and existing seller relationships in mobiles and electronics have helped Minutes differentiate itself from other quick-commerce platforms. At the same time, the company is expanding Minutes’ fresh category alongside beauty, personal care and other immediate-use categories.
Minutes has now expanded to more than 1,000 dark stores across 120-130 cities. The all-India network averages around 800-1,000 orders per store per day, while mature stores can reach 1,200-1,500 orders per day within five to six months of launch.
Minutes’ advertising revenue is broadly comparable with other leading quick-commerce platforms, according to the UBS expert. Gross margins are improving but remain below Blinkit’s levels, while city-level economics are expected to improve as markets mature. Store and city maturity will remain important drivers of Minutes’ margin trajectory.
With order values nearing Blinkit’s levels, advertising revenue broadly in line with leading peers and a higher overall basket when mobile orders are included, Minutes’ category mix could remain an important differentiator as Flipkart expands its quick-commerce footprint.
Blinkit, meanwhile, continues to lead the quick-commerce market on user reach. Its share of tracked monthly active users stood at 38% in July, up 31 basis points month-on-month and 375 basis points year-on-year. Rentomojo, the Accel-backed furniture and appliance rental platform, has filed its Red Herring Prospectus (RHP) for its initial public offering (IPO).
The Bengaluru-based company is looking to raise around Rs 1,255.6 crore through the IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of Rs 150 crore and an offer-for-sale (OFS) of around 2.73 crore shares worth Rs 1,105.6 crore.
The company has fixed a price band of Rs 384-404 per share, valuing Rentomojo at around Rs 4,200 crore at the upper end. The IPO will open for subscription on September 9 and close on September 11, while anchor investors can bid on September 8.
Existing investors, including Accel India, Edelweiss, IDG Ventures India, ValueQuest, Madison India and GMO, along with founder Geetansh Bamania, will sell shares through the OFS.
Rentomojo plans to use the fresh issue proceeds primarily to strengthen its balance sheet. About Rs 70 crore will go towards debt repayment, while another Rs 42.5 crore will be used for lease rentals and licence fees for its warehouses and experience stores.
According to the company’s DRHP, Accel India is the largest shareholder with a 20.92% stake, followed by founder Geetansh Bamania and Chiratae Ventures with 14.69% and 13.69%, respectively. Edelweiss Discovery Fund holds 10.53%, while ValueQuest S.C.A.L.E Fund commands 8.92%. 
Financially, Rentomojo has continued to grow while remaining profitable. Its revenue from operations rose 45.5% year-on-year to Rs 387 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 266 crore in FY25. Profit after tax jumped 142% to R 104.2 crore from Rs 43.1 crore in the previous fiscal.
As of March 2026, Rentomojo had 2.54 lakh live subscribers across 29 cities. The company operates through 20 warehouses and 82 experience stores.

Its current programmes focus on sleep, VO₂ Max and glucose metabolism. Other features include AFib Detection, Cycle & Ovulation Pro and cardiovascular fitness age, along with PowerPlugs for additional health-related capabilities.
Ultrahuman reported Rs 565 crore in revenue and Rs 73 crore profit after tax in FY25. The company had projected revenue of around Rs 1,000 crore for FY26 as it looked to expand further in international markets.
